The essence of a layoff is the act of admitting that the company failed to keep its promise to its employees. You tell someone you hired by saying, 'We will hire you and you will thrive here,' that 'I am sorry, but the company no longer has the resources to support you.' This is not a matter of numbers; it is a matter of trust.

If the executive does not admit this fact and says it is 'the economy's fault' or 'the market's fault,' the employees will see through it. They will think, 'This management team does not admit their own judgment errors and is pushing the responsibility onto the people on the front lines.' That is where trust collapses.

This is because when you ask people to leave, you are not just being watched by those who are leaving. The people who remain are watching everything, too. 'How did the company treat those who left?' 'Did the leader speak honestly?' 'Did they try to deceive us?'—the remaining employees will remember these things, and they will work under the shadow of those memories for years to come.
The same thing happened at Horowitz's company. Because the way they handled the layoffs was sincere, the remaining employees felt they could trust the company and were able to overcome the crisis.

Because focus is concentrated on how to handle those who are leaving, communication with those who remain is often put on the back burner. As a result, the remaining employees are left in a state of uncertainty. 'I wasn't affected this time, but will there be a next time?' 'What is the company thinking?'—these anxieties erode the organization.

A mass email arrives from the HR department. Top management makes an announcement in a large hall. Subordinates find out whether they were affected by checking an email or a list—this approach may look efficient, but it wounds the organization most deeply.

The amount of dialogue the CEO or leaders have with those who remain in the weeks following a layoff announcement shows the company's level of seriousness. If employees are left alone with the thought that 'it's fine because I wasn't targeted,' the anxiety of those remaining will quietly erode the organization.

A layoff is not just a task of reducing numbers. It is a litmus test for institutional design and humanity, where the company acknowledges it failed to keep its promises and protects the dignity of both those who leave and those who remain.
"Due to deteriorating performance, we have announced a reduction in force."

Behind this single line in the news, what does the executive think, what do they prepare, and how do they communicate it? The quality of the design of that entire process will have a long-lasting impact on the company's future.

Ben Horowitz experienced three layoffs during his time at Loudcloud/Opsware. In particular, the pivot from Loudcloud to Opsware involved a reduction of 400 people. At first, it was trial and error, and it was painful.
But from that experience, he began to rethink layoffs not as a 'necessary evil,' but as the moment where a leader's integrity is most tested.
